appraisal_events.evidence: l'auteur de ce livre sur Whistler... est souvent rendu avec une grande délicatesse par l'amoureux de tous les raffinements, de toutes les joliesses de la chose peinte qu'est Verdurin; and Verdurin's own claim, 'vous savez bien, et Gautier le savait aussi, que mes salons étaient autre chose que ces piteux Maîtres d'autrefois crus un chef-d'œuvre dans la famille de ma femme,' offered against guests who took him for wholly inferior to Charles Blanc, Saint-Victor, Sainte-Beuve, Burty.
appraisal_events.explanation: Goncourt's diary lavishly praises Verdurin as a refined connoisseur and writer underestimated by his own salon's guests, elevating him within the quoted account; but the frame narrator has just voiced doubt that literature reveals 'vérité profonde,' casting this admiring portrait in an ironic light.

status_effects.explanation: Goncourt's account presents Verdurin as a serious, delicately perceptive connoisseur and author who is locally misjudged as inferior by his own guests, raising his portrayed standing, though the ironic frame around Goncourt's judgment tempers this.

As hostess of the same admiringly described salon and table (rare masterwork vases, exquisite chrysanthemum display), she shares in the elevated portrayal by association, though she is never named directly in this excerpt.

ambiguities: The admiring description of the Verdurin salon is Goncourt's own quoted diary voice; it is uncertain how far the frame narrator endorses rather than ironizes this portrait, especially given his immediately preceding doubt that literature reveals 'vérité profonde' -- a passage generally read as a pastiche of Goncourt's style.
Mme Verdurin is identified only implicitly, as 'la maîtresse de la maison' and through the couple's shared hôtel, not by name, in this excerpt.
